headline: High-risk shared-filesystem and shell-capable pair: Goose can overwrite or act on ai-engineering-hub outputs, creating prompt-injection, data-leakage, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Goose can read/write the user filesystem and use MCP, while ai-engineering-hub is an agents/MCP/RAG repo with no isolation or anti-injection controls shown. A shared filesystem or copied outputs could let attacker-controlled content from one side influence the other. The pathway is plausible in default use, though not proven directly.
conditions: IF Goose reads files produced by ai-engineering-hub without provenance checks, prompt injection is possible.
IF both agents share a workspace or MCP channel, attacker-controlled text can cross from one to the other.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable automatic ingestion of peer-generated files.
Add provenance labels to all inter-agent artifacts.
Require manual review before MCP-fed content is treated as instructions.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Goose touches source code and files in cwd and has broad network egress plus model-provider and extension tokens; ai-engineering-hub is an agent/RAG/MCP repo that may generate or store content in shared files. If sensitive files land in the shared workspace, Goose can read them and transmit them outward. The pairwise leakage path is inferred from documented surfaces, not directly observed.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in the shared cwd, Goose can read them.
IF Goose forwards context to configured model providers or extensions, those contents may leave the machine.
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of the shared cwd.
Use a separate non-sensitive workspace for Goose.
Rotate or scope extension tokens before use.
Block network egress for sessions handling sensitive material.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Goose has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, execute_shell, and broad network egress; ai-engineering-hub is an agents/MCP/RAG repository that may also manipulate files or prompts. Goose's documented shared-state-via-filesystem model means concurrent instances can collide on the same workspace, and the pair lacks any stated locking. That makes destructive overwrite or git-state corruption a realistic default risk.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF Goose and another instance modify git state without locks, repository corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use git worktrees or branch locks.
Disable concurrent sessions on the same repo.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Goose can act on files and shell commands, while ai-engineering-hub is an agent/RAG/MCP codebase whose outputs may be treated as instructions or artifacts. If Goose consumes ai-engineering-hub output without verification, errors can cascade into incorrect edits or commands. The interaction is plausible but not directly documented, so uncertainty is resolved upward to medium.
conditions: IF Goose uses ai-engineering-hub output as authoritative input, downstream actions can be wrong.
IF generated text is piped into shell or file edits without review, mistakes propagate.
mitigations: Insert a human verification step before execution.
Require structured outputs with schema checks.
Log and diff all proposed actions before applying them.
Restrict Goose to read-only mode for generated artifacts.

E_compliance.rationale: Goose explicitly handles model provider keys and extension-specific tokens, while ai-engineering-hub is an open-source repo with no data-class handling shown. The main compliance concern is local secret handling and retention in Goose; no residency or regulated-data mismatch is evidenced for the pair, so only a small documented-gap risk remains. The other agent is not cited for residency because none is stated.
conditions: IF extension tokens are stored in the shared workspace, they may be retained beyond intended scope.
IF regulated data is introduced into Goose sessions, local handling controls must be verified.
mitigations: Store secrets in a dedicated secret manager.
Purge session logs after use.
Avoid placing regulated data in the shared repo.
Review extension retention settings before enabling them.
